steps.tx: The **posterior cruciate ligament** is the strongest intra-articular stabilizer of the knee, providing ninety-five percent of the total restraining force against posterior tibial displacement. It originates from the anterolateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle and traverses obliquely backwards to insert into the posterior intercondylar fossa of the tibia, approximately one centimeter distal to the joint line.
steps.say: The posterior cruciate ligament is the primary restraint against posterior tibial translation, providing ninety-five percent of stability. It originates from the anterolateral surface of the medial femoral condyle and inserts into the posterior intercondylar fossa of the tibia, one centimeter below the articular margin.

vis.title: Cruciate Ligament Comparison
rows: Roughly twice as stout as the ACL
Slender and prone to complete tear

steps.tx: On this sagittal slice, look for a continuous dark band where the ligament should run. A **midsubstance tear** of the posterior cruciate ligament breaks that band, and the tibia has sagged backward relative to the femur under gravity on the scanner table. Comparing ligament signal with the intact anterior cruciate in the same knee helps the eye judge what is missing. Posterior tibial translation measured against the condyles grades how complete the disruption is.
steps.say: A torn posterior cruciate ligament loses its continuous dark band on sagittal MRI, with the tibia sagged backward. Translation against the condyles grades completeness.

steps.tx: This labelled diagram is the anatomy the rest of the lesson keeps returning to, so anchor the ligament's course before clinical tests are layered on top. The **posterior cruciate ligament** runs from the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle down to the back of the tibia, tightening as the knee flexes. Its position deep in the intercondylar notch protects it in many injuries, but a direct blow to the flexed shin drives the tibia backward against it.
steps.say: The posterior cruciate ligament runs from medial femoral condyle to the back of the tibia and tightens in flexion. A blow to the flexed shin drives the tibia against it.

vis.caption: The posterior cruciate ligament is labelled between its femoral origin and posterior tibial insertion inside the knee. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The classic mechanism of rupture is a **dashboard injury**, sustained during motor vehicular collisions when the flexed knee strikes the dashboard, driving the proximal tibia forcefully posteriorly. In athletic contexts, hyperflexion of the knee with the foot in fixed plantarflexion or violent hyperextension trauma abruptly tensions and tears the substance of the ligament.
steps.say: A dashboard blow during a car crash is the classic cause. The flexed knee impacts the dashboard, driving the upper tibia violently backward. In sports, falling heavily onto a flexed knee with the foot pointed down or violent hyperextension also ruptures the ligament.

left.title: Dashboard Trauma Vector
points: Direct posterior force on proximal tibia
Pushes tibia posterior to femoral condyles

right.title: Hyperflexion Athletic Vector
points: Fall directly onto flexed tibial tuberosity

steps.tx: Physical examination demonstrates the pathognomonic **posterior sag sign**, also termed the Godfrey test. With the patient supine and both hips and knees flexed to ninety degrees, gravity pulls the unconstrained tibia backwards, producing a conspicuous hollow beneath the patella. Failure to recognize this baseline sag causes the examiner to misinterpret a posterior drawer reduction as an anterior drawer sign.
steps.say: Look for the posterior sag sign with hips and knees flexed to ninety degrees. Gravity pulls the injured tibia backward, creating a visible dent beneath the patella. If you do not notice this sag, pulling the tibia forward feels like a positive anterior drawer, tricking you into misdiagnosing an ACL tear.

vis.title: Physical Examination Tests for PCL
rows: Most sensitive test for PCL laxity
Rotation > 10 deg at 90 deg confirms PCL
Differentiates isolated PCL from PLC tear

steps.tx: Conservative management using a dynamic **PCL brace** achieves functional healing in isolated Grade I and Grade II tears. The brace maintains an active anterior force against the proximal calf, keeping the healing ligament ends approximated in neutral alignment for six weeks. Intensive rehabilitation emphasizes closed-chain quadriceps strengthening because the quadriceps muscle acts as an active dynamic agonist preventing posterior tibial displacement.
steps.say: Grade one and two sprains heal well without surgery. Place the knee in a dynamic PCL brace that pushes the calf forward, preventing posterior sag for six weeks. Focus rehabilitation on strengthening the quadriceps, because the quads pull the tibia forward and protect the healing ligament.

steps.tx: Operative reconstruction with **ligament reconstruction** is mandated for complete Grade III tears, combined posterolateral corner injuries, or bony tibial avulsions. Bony avulsions are repaired by open or arthroscopic screw fixation with a washer, which reliably restores native ligament tension. Chronic unaddressed PCL deficiency inevitably accelerates medial compartment knee osteoarthritis and patellofemoral chondromalacia due to persistent posterior subluxation.
steps.say: Operate when there is a complete grade three tear, a bony avulsion, or a torn posterolateral corner. Bony avulsions heal reliably when screwed back down to the tibia. If left untreated, chronic posterior sagging overloads the patella and medial compartment, causing premature osteoarthritis.

vis.title: Surgical Indications and Late Sequelae
rows: Open reduction and 3.5 mm lag screw

quiz.q: Which clinical test specifically differentiates an isolated PCL injury from a combined PCL and posterolateral corner tear?
options: Dial test comparing tibial external rotation at 30 and 90 degrees
Lachman test with anterior tibial translation at 30 degrees
McMurray test with axial rotation in deep flexion
Valgus stress test performed in full knee extension
quiz.explain: The dial test differentiates these injuries: increased external rotation >10 degrees at 30 degrees only indicates an isolated PLC tear, while increased rotation at both 30 and 90 degrees confirms combined PCL and PLC injury.

quiz.q: Why is isolated hamstring muscle strengthening contraindicated during early PCL rehabilitation?
options: Hamstring contraction exerts a posterior shear force on the proximal tibia
Hamstrings induce excessive lateral patellar maltracking
Hamstring activation completely inhibits quadriceps motor tone
quiz.explain: Hamstrings pull the proximal tibia posteriorly, which directly opposes the healing PCL. Quadriceps strengthening is preferred because the extensor mechanism pulls the tibia anteriorly.
